title: Confrontation Standard
summary: Confrontation means addressing disagreement or inappropriate behaviour respectfully to protect the standard and find a professional solution — never to attack, embarrass, or overpower another person.

sections.title: The Standard
paragraphs: Confrontation refers to directly addressing a disagreement, concern, conflict, or inappropriate behaviour with a colleague, leader, or client. At Zura Spa, confrontation should never be about attacking, embarrassing, or overpowering another person. It should be about addressing issues respectfully, protecting the standard, and finding a professional solution.

sections.title: 1. No Confrontations
paragraphs: Frequent or poorly handled confrontations are unhealthy for a workplace because they create tension, fear, resentment, and unnecessary divisions among team members. When disagreements are handled through anger, shouting, insults, or personal attacks, communication breaks down and staff may become defensive rather than solution-focused. This can negatively affect teamwork, productivity, morale, and ultimately the client's experience.
At Zura Spa, concerns should be addressed calmly, respectfully, and through the proper channels, with the goal of resolving the issue rather than creating another one.

sections.title: 2. The Therapist's Mindset
paragraphs: Before confronting an issue, the therapist should ask: "Am I trying to solve the problem, or am I trying to prove that I am right?"

sections.title: Stay Calm
paragraphs: Do not begin a confrontation while angry or emotionally overwhelmed.

sections.title: Focus on the Issue
paragraphs: Address the specific behaviour or situation—not the person's character.

sections.title: Seek Understanding
paragraphs: Do not assume you know someone's intention. Clarify what happened first.

sections.title: Be Respectful
paragraphs: You can be firm without being rude or aggressive.

sections.title: Be Solution-Focused
paragraphs: The goal should be to determine what needs to happen next.

sections.title: Be Accountable
paragraphs: If you contributed to the problem, be willing to acknowledge it.

sections.title: Know When to Escalate
paragraphs: Not every confrontation should be handled personally. Serious, sensitive, threatening, or unresolved matters should be taken to the appropriate supervisor or management.

sections.title: 3. What Therapists Should Not Do
list: Shout or scream at another person.
Insult, threaten, intimidate, or humiliate anyone.
Confront someone aggressively in front of clients or other unnecessary people.
Physically touch, block, threaten, or intimidate someone during a disagreement.
Turn a workplace issue into a personal attack.
Bring up unrelated past issues simply to win an argument.
Make accusations without understanding the facts.
Spread the issue through gossip before or after addressing it.
Encourage other staff to take sides.
Post workplace conflicts on social media.
Confront a client aggressively when the matter should be escalated to management.
Continue an argument when the other person is becoming highly emotional or aggressive.
Retaliate against someone because they raised a concern.
Use confrontation as a way to settle personal grudges.
Allow a confrontation to interfere with a client's session or experience.

sections.title: 4. How to Approach a Confrontation
paragraphs: Where appropriate, use: OBSERVE → CLARIFY → COMMUNICATE → SOLVE → ESCALATE.
Observe: Understand what actually happened.
Clarify: Ask questions before making conclusions.
Communicate: Explain the concern calmly and respectfully.
Solve: Agree on what should happen going forward.
Escalate: If the issue is serious, unresolved, or outside your authority, involve the appropriate leader.
Instead of: "You are always disrespectful and difficult to work with."
Say: "I felt uncomfortable with how that conversation happened earlier. Can we clarify what happened so we can handle similar situations better going forward?"
The second approach addresses the behaviour and solution, rather than attacking the individual.

sections.title: 5. The Zura Confrontation Mindset
paragraphs: Every therapist should remember:
"I can be firm without being aggressive."
"I can address a problem without attacking a person."
"I can disagree without disrespecting."
"I can receive confrontation without immediately becoming defensive."
"If I cannot resolve it professionally, I will escalate it appropriately."

sections.title: Zura Standard
paragraphs: DON'T ATTACK. DON'T SHOUT. DON'T GOSSIP. DON'T RETALIATE. DON'T ASSUME.
CLARIFY. COMMUNICATE. STAY CALM. FOCUS ON SOLUTIONS. ESCALATE WHEN NECESSARY.
At Zura Spa, we don't avoid problems—we address them with maturity, respect, and a solution-based mindset.

remember: Be firm without being aggressive. Address the issue, not the person. Escalate when you cannot resolve it professionally.
